newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Focus on ECI.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Focus on ECI.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices are expected to remain stuck in narrow ranges Tuesday, although the day's economic reports should boost trading activity.
Market participants noted that the handful of data won't go unnoticed -- but they aren't likely to move prices much.

"You can't do much ahead of the (October) employment report" on Friday, said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities. "If you see unfavorable numbers, how much can you sell ahead of payrolls? And if you see favorable numbers how much can you buy?"
Still, players cited the third-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI), due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, as the key number. The market is centering on a 0.8-percent rise in the ECI.

The ECI is "a figure that can move the market," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "The market wants to see if labor markets are heating up enough to give a significant boost to compensation, which we haven't seen yet."
Also scheduled for release Tuesday is the BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales report at 0900 EST/1400 GMT.
In addition, the market will absorb The Conference Board's consumer confidence report for October at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, and Redbook retail sales at 1455 EST/1955 GMT.
The retail numbers are seen as non-events, while consumer confidence is also expected to have limited impact on trading.
"We got strong consumer confidence Friday and no one cared," said Kevin Sluder, a trader at First Chicago Capital Markets, referring to the University of Michigan report.
After a light day on Monday, participants expect a pickup in activity, albeit a limited one. Retail is still on the sidelines, leaving central banks as the prime participants.
Meanwhile, the dollar's rise above 114 yen should be bullish for Treasuries, players said.
Traders said the bond should trade between 6.75 percent and 6.90 percent until Friday morning, even if the data come as a surprise and stray from market expectations.

With most investors content with their positions, since there is no clear direction to the economy, traders said it will take a big event -- such as a surprise in the election or in the payroll data -- to force investors to change their view on the economy and Federal Reserve policy.
